To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) rats can be trained to make long runs of responses, (b) the acquisition of such runs is facilitated by the use of a targeted percentile procedure, and (c) this procedure is effective in producing long runs even though it does not increase reinforcement rate or overall reinforcement probability.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of differential reinforcement of response rate and the acquisition of response rate.
the acquisition and maintenance of behavior in a situation in which the reinforcement contingencies are not molar but instead are local.
the acquisition of response differentiation in the context of a continuing reinforcement schedule.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current results do not support molar formulations, but they do not disconfirm them either.

the results are consistent with a model in which the probability of a response on a given trial is determined by the probability of a reinforcer on that trial, but that the probability of a given reinforcer is a function not only of the number of responses on that trial but also of the number of previous responses on the same side as the current response.
the current experiment provides no support for molar models, while providing strong support for the importance of local contingencies in shaping and controlling behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reinforcement rate is the primary determinant of response rate, but that the number of responses required to obtain reinforcement is the primary determinant for the form of responding.
molar reinforcement models are not sufficient to describe the effects of differential reinforcement of run length.
reinforcement is a powerful motivator of behavior, but it is a poor determinant of behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reinforcement rate, reinforcement frequency, and reinforcement probability per response are not sufficient to predict behavior in a complex schedule.
the reinforcement contingencies that are in effect at the moment of behavior exert an enormous influence on behavior.

the molar approach is inadequate to account for even the most elementary aspects of operant behavior, and that the local approach is necessary to understand how behavior changes in response to reinforcement contingencies.
